Pusillanimous

pyoo-suh-LAN-uh-muhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Pusillanimous is lacking courage or determination; cowardly.

Historians called the general's decision to retreat without a fight pusillanimous, a stain on an otherwise proud military career.

Worked Example

The board's pusillanimous refusal to confront the failing CEO cost the company another two years of losses.

Being too cowardly to make a difficult but necessary decision is exactly what pusillanimous describes.

How Pusillanimous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

cowardly

cowardly: lacking courage; shamefully afraid

spineless

spineless: lacking the will to stand up for oneself

Antonyms

courageous

courageous: able to face danger or difficulty with bravery

bold

bold: confident and willing to take risks

How Strong Is It? — cowardly → pusillanimous → spineless

cowardly vs. pusillanimous

cowardly vs. pusillanimous: Slipping out the back door to avoid the angry customer was a cowardly move, but at least it was a one-time lapse.

spineless vs. pusillanimous

spineless vs. pusillanimous: Everyone in the office knew the manager was spineless -- he caved to every complaint and never once backed up his own staff.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of pusillanimous.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pusill-

root — pusill-: very small, weak (Latin)

root — anim-

root — anim-: spirit, mind, soul (Latin)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin pusillus ('very small, petty') plus animus ('spirit, mind') plus -ous ('having the quality of') -- pusillanimous literally means 'small-spirited,' too weak-spirited to face danger or make a hard choice.

Use the root in a new word: unanimous

Use the root in a new word: unanimous: The jury reached a unanimous decision after just twenty minutes of deliberation.

Root Check

Word Choice

Pusillanimous is a strong, almost scornful word -- reserve it for judging a decision or a person's character as shamefully cowardly, not just for describing ordinary nervousness. Compare it with timorous, which describes fearfulness itself rather than a moral failing, and diffident, which is about social self-doubt rather than fear of danger at all.
